title: Chapter 174 – Tide Season
html:
[The Gate Stair – Tian Mo]

The bell rings from the Garden Hall at dusk, and Tian Mo, on the fifth landing, hears it as a man in a well hears a stone drop.

It is a flat, hard, clanging peal, struck six times and then six times again, and he has never heard it rung except in practice. Six and six. Danger below. The old code, from the Founders' day, when the Garden had a stair and a dock and a wall of black stone, and nobody could say what was on the other side.

He does not move. He stands as he has stood every dawn and every dusk for twenty-three years, with his staff planted before him and his knees bent a little and his weight on the balls of his feet. His eyes are on the dark below. The stair runs down from the landing in a long steep spiral, seven hundred and one steps to the Dock, lit by blue lamps in niches along the wall. Most are guttering. All of them are trembling.

The floor of the stair has begun to hum.

He has felt it since noon. A fine thin shiver in the stone, which he took for a passing cart. It has grown all afternoon, into a beat, into a drone, and now, as the bell dies away above him, into a sound he can only describe as a throat clearing. A deep, vast, patient clearing of the throat, from somewhere under the mountain, from somewhere at the bottom of the world.

They have to come through you, Kuang said.

Tian Mo breathes in. He lets it out slowly, through the nose. He puts his weight down.

"Right," he says, to no one. "Let them."

* * *

The runner reaches him an hour later, a Garden boy of fifteen with a flushed face and a smear of orchard soil down one sleeve.

"Warden." He bows too fast and has to catch himself on the rail. "Clan Head Zhao says the orchard is lost. The crawlers came up through the roots at dusk, from under the old terraces. The guards pulled back to the Garden wall and they are holding there. She says..." He stops and swallows. He has memorized it, and it comes out in a rush. "She says they are not interested in the wall. They go around it. They are all going the same way, toward the Mother Tree, and the only road beneath the tree is your stair."

Tian Mo takes this in without moving his face. "Casualties?"

"Eleven dead at the orchard. More hurt. Nobody counted yet."

"The Sect line at the Pass?"

"Head Han's pupils are holding. A runner came from the north an hour ago. The Valley Wall is shaking, but it stands." The boy hesitates. "And Warden. There is no word from Lin Jian."

"There wouldn't be." Tian Mo's tone is mild. "He has a long way to climb."

"Yes, Warden."

"Go back and tell Clan Head Zhao the fifth landing is held. Tell her it will stay held. And boy." The runner turns. "Eat something. Then find a bucket and carry water. Everyone carries something tonight. That is how a house survives."

The boy bows again, properly this time, and goes.

Tian Mo stands a little longer in the lamplight, looking at the place where the boy's footsteps fade. He is thirty-four years old. He has been the Warden of the Stair for twenty-three of them, ever since the old Warden, a man called Hu, who taught him to stand, set a dying hand on his shoulder and said, You are the stair now. He has never married. He has never left the Garden for longer than a season. The villagers in the lower terraces think him a gloomy, silent man, and he has never troubled to correct them.

Gloomy, he thinks. Perhaps.

But a stair needs someone who does not leave.

* * *

At the foot of the landing, in the niche where the first blue lamp burns, the stone creature opens its eyes.

It has sat there for as long as anyone remembers: a squat gray figure carved from the same black rock as the Gate wall, no taller than a child, with long arms and a blunt blank face. The Garden children call it Grandfather Pebble and leave it offerings of sugared plums. In twenty-three years, Tian Mo has never seen it move.

Now it rises. It does so slowly, with a grinding like a millstone turning, and a little rain of dust sifts off its shoulders. The eyes are two chips of pale light. It looks at him. Then it steps onto the landing beside him and plants itself, feet apart, in the exact stance he has taught a thousand pupils.

Behind him, the guards stop breathing.

"Well," says Tian Mo, after a moment. "I thought you might be furniture."

The creature says nothing. It turns its blunt face down the stair. A low hum rises from its chest, the same note the stone has been humming all afternoon, and Tian Mo understands, with a small unexpected tightening in his throat, that it has been waiting all this time for the same thing he has. Not for a fight. For the moment when standing means something.

"Stay on my left," he tells it.

It shifts one grinding step, and does.

* * *

They come up the stair at the second hour of the night.

He hears them long before he sees them. Tick, tick, tick. The thin dry sound of hooked legs on stone, a hundred paces below, in the bend where the blue light fails. It is not loud. It is almost delicate. It is the sound of something that does not need to hurry, because it is certain of where it is going.

He has forty with him.

They are the best the Garden has: forty men and women in quilted gowns, on the landings above, with spears and short swords and a case of crossbow bolts apiece. They came at a run when Zhao rang the bell. They are grim and white-faced and silent, and when he turns his head he can see the same thought in every face. We are the last door. The stair is the Garden's throat. If it is breached, the beasts will come up into the cellars, and the cellars hold seven hundred children.

"Remember," he says. His voice is low and flat, and it carries. "You do not go forward. You do not step off your landing. If something gets past me, you kill it, and then you go back to where you stood."

A murmur.

"The stair is narrow. They have to come single file. The first one is mine." He lifts the staff an inch. "When I fall back, you fall back one landing. Not before. Is that understood?"

"Understood," they say.

He nods. He turns to the dark.

The sound has changed. The ticking is closer, and louder, and behind it there is a second sound, a wet slithering, as of something very large and soft hauling itself up out of the pit. A smell rises. It is cold iron, and rot, and the sour musk of a thing that has been a long time underground. The nearest of the blue lamps goes out.

He sets his feet.

* * *

The first crawler is the size of a calf, and he kills it in three moves.

It comes around the bend in a rush, a pale wet blur of legs, and he does not step to meet it. He lets it come. The staff snaps out in a short low arc and takes the front leg at the joint. The beast stumbles. The second blow comes down on the bone ring, a single hard crack, and the flat blind head folds like an egg. It slides back down the stair in a heap of twitching legs and is gone.

"One," says someone, behind him. A woman. Her voice shakes.

"One," he agrees.

The second comes at once. And the third. They are small, as crawlers go. Juvenile. Quick and mindless and thin-skinned, boiling up the stair in a pale flood, and he stands in the narrow place and the staff goes out and returns, out and returns, and the pile of broken limbs on the step below him grows.

Stand, said Kuang. That's the whole of it.

It is a trick, he knows. It is not a technique, in any Sect's sense. There is no breath-art in it, no fold, no flash. It is only that he is a man in a corridor, and the corridor is one body wide, and anything that wishes to pass must go through him. He does not have to be the strongest. He only has to be the last.

A Gnasher appears.

It is bigger. A great barrel of a beast, dark gray, with a mouth like a trap, that comes up the stair on its belly and takes the stone in its jaws as it climbs. Tian Mo drops his staff low and braces. It strikes his guard with a force that jars his arms to the shoulders and drives him back a half step, and then another. The stone cracks under his heel.

"Fall back!" he shouts. "One landing!"

The forty above him shuffle up. He holds.

Beneath the Gnasher's jaws, something clicks, like a latch. He sees its eyes, small and red and quite without malice, and he thinks: It is only hungry. He ducks the snap, and rolls, and drives the butt of the staff down on the beast's skull with every ounce of his weight.

It goes still.

He is breathing hard. He steps back onto his landing and plants his feet. His forearms are numb.

"Two hundred," says the woman behind him, faintly. "I counted. That was two hundred."

"Keep counting."

"There are more."

"Yes," he says. "There always are."

* * *

The hours before midnight are the worst, because they are the longest.

The crawlers keep coming, and the guards keep killing them, and the pile of broken bodies on the steps below the fifth landing grows until it begins to slide. Twice Tian Mo orders the dead cleared with hooks, and twice the guards do it with a grim, dogged efficiency, wading ankle-deep in black blood. A young man named Pol goes down with a leg opened to the bone. They haul him up the stair by his collar, and he is silent, and his face is the color of tallow. A woman at the rear takes a Gnasher's bite across the shoulder and keeps her spear in both hands, and will not be taken off her landing until Tian Mo walks up and takes the spear himself.

"I can hold," she says through her teeth.

"I know you can." He sets the spear against the wall. "That is why you are going to live."

By the eleventh hour he has stopped feeling his hands. By the twelfth, he has stopped counting the dead. There is only the stair, and the staff, and the small hard bright point of the next breath.

He thinks of Kuang, thirteen years old, with a brown wooden sword and the same stubborn look the boy's father had worn at the same age. Why do you stand? the boy asked him, one evening in the autumn, as the bell rang for supper. Doesn't it hurt?

Yes, Tian Mo said. Every day.

Then why?

He had not had an answer then. He is not sure he has one now. But in the dark, with the ticking rising out of the pit, he finds a kind of answer in the shape of the thing itself: that someone has to be the place where it stops. That the world is full of people running, and a world needs, somewhere in it, a person who does not.

He is not brave. He has always known that. He is only unable to leave.

It turns out, tonight, that this is enough.

At midnight, the roots come.

He does not understand at first. It begins as a creak in the stone, a long wooden groan that seems to come from inside the wall. The blue lamps flicker. A fine dust sifts down from the ceiling. Then, between two of the great blocks of the stair, a crack opens, no wider than a finger, and something pale and slender pushes out into the lamplight.

It is a root.

It is white and fine as a hair, and it feels at the air like a blind thing, and where it touches the stone, the stone yields. More come. A second crack, a third. Pale tendrils spill out of the walls, the ceiling, the floor, a hundred, a thousand, creeping down the steps in a slow silent tide. The guards behind him cry out. A man drops his spear.

"Hold!" Tian Mo's voice cracks like a whip. "Hold your places!"

The roots flow past him.

They do not touch him. They do not touch the guards. They slide around his boots, around the staff, around the huddled forms on the upper landings, and spill down the stair toward the dark. He watches, rigid, as the nearest of the crawlers comes around the bend, and the roots rise to meet it.

They take it like a spider takes a fly.

Pale coils lash round the thrashing legs. They tighten. They pull. The crawler screams, a thin high wail, and is drawn backward into the wall, and the stone closes over it as water closes over a pebble. Another follows. Another. The sound of the ticking changes to a sound of snapping, and then to a wet silence.

"The tree," whispers the woman behind him.

He has never seen it. He has only been told. But he knows, with a knowledge that goes down to the soles of his feet, what he is looking at: the Mother Tree, which Qinghe planted and Wenyuan tended and the whole Garden has loved for a hundred years, reaching down through the soil and the stone to the aid of the one who stands in its stair.

It's an anchor, he thinks. That's what Jian meant. It is the thing that holds the Garden to the ground.

Overhead, faintly, through all that earth, he hears a voice. It is singing.

* * *

The guards get a rest, of sorts. Qinghe sends food.

It comes down the stair at the third hour, carried in covered pots by four sturdy kitchen girls in white aprons, who pass the roots with a visible shudder and a visible determination not to scream. Rice and pickled radish. Tea in a black iron kettle. A pile of steamed buns, each as big as a fist. The girls set it all on the landing, bow, and flee up the stair.

The guards fall on it. Tian Mo does not. He stands where he is, with his staff across his shoulders, watching the dark.

"You should eat," says the woman behind him. She is a short, stout, red-faced guard named Dai, who has been stationed at the Garden gate for twelve years, and who is holding out a bun. "I mean it. You've been standing since dawn."

"I stand."

"I know. But you can stand and chew."

He looks at the bun. It is still hot. It smells of lard and pork and ginger, and his stomach turns over.

He takes it. It is the best thing he has ever eaten.

"She does that on purpose, you know," says Dai, watching him. "Qinghe. She can't taste a thing. So she puts in everything she can think of, and trusts the rest of us to tell her. I swear I could eat a bucket of her buns."

"She's remarkable."

"She's terrifying." Dai grins. "I'd follow her into a Rank-3 beast's mouth."

"I think she would."

They laugh. It's a short laugh, short and raw. But it breaks something in the dark.

Down the line, a man starts to hum. It is an old tune, a harvest song, the kind sung over the threshing floor, and a second voice picks it up, and then a third. Nobody sings the words. They only hum, low and tuneless, forty people on a stone stair with blood on their sleeves and a hot bun in each hand. Tian Mo does not join. He has never had a voice for it. But he lets the sound settle over his shoulders like a blanket, and he finds that his hands have stopped shaking.

Above, through a hundred feet of earth, the other song answers. The lullaby. Slow and wordless, in a voice that is neither a man's nor a woman's, and the roots in the wall sway to it as wheat sways in a wind.

"Do you hear that?" Dai asks softly.

"Yes."

"Is it the tree?"

"I think," Tian Mo says, "that it is everyone who ever sat under it."

She does not answer. After a while, she hums too.

* * *

Toward dawn, the Gate wall speaks.

He feels it first in his chest. A deep resonance, a bass note below sound, rising up the stair from the Dock. The roots go rigid. The blue lamps flare and die. And from the black stone at the bottom of the world, seven hundred and one steps beneath his feet, there comes a voice.

It is not loud. It is not human. It is a vast patient cold voice, like the voice of a river under ice, and it says, in a language he does not know and understands perfectly:

Stand.

Tian Mo's hands tighten on the staff.

Stand, says the wall. The door is opening. The last of them are coming through.

"Who?" he calls. His voice cracks in the dark. "Who is coming?"

All of them. The voice is calm. The ones who were never meant to wake. Stand, Warden. Stand until the keeper comes. It will not be long.

He stares down the stair. He sees nothing. But the roots are drawing back now, in a slow rustling wave, like grass bending in a wind, and from the dark below, from the bend where the blue light dies, there comes a sound he has not heard before. It is not ticking. It is not slithering. It is something heavier. A scrape. A thud. A sound like a very large door being dragged across a very large floor.

Dai has come up behind him. She is white to the lips.

"What is it?" she whispers.

"I don't know."

"Is it the end?"

"I think," says Tian Mo slowly, "that it is the middle."

* * *

The Rider comes up the stair at first light.

It is the largest thing he has seen. It fills the bend like a cork fills a bottle, a thing of dark mottled hide and ridged bone, with six jointed limbs and a long blunt head, and on its back, strapped in some filthy harness of sinew and iron, a rider: a pale naked figure, hairless, eyeless, with a mouth full of needles. The beast's breath comes in a long steaming rumble. It stops at the foot of the last flight, and the rider lifts its head, and sniffs.

Tian Mo feels the guards behind him go cold.

Rank-2, he thinks. At least. Perhaps more. He knows what the Founders' histories say about the Riders. Beasts that have been bent to someone's will. Beasts with a master. He glances at the roots, drawn back into the walls in a trembling hush, as though the tree itself were afraid.

"Back," he says quietly. "All of you. Up to the second landing."

"Tian—" begins Dai.

"Go."

"We can't leave you."

"You are not leaving. You are holding the next one." His voice is as flat and calm as it has ever been. "I'll hold this. Go."

They go. He hears the scrape of their boots on the stone, the muffled cries, the long retreat. He does not turn. He stands alone on the fifth landing with his staff planted and his knees bent, in the faint dying blue light, and looks down at the thing that is looking up at him.

The rider smiles.

It speaks. Its voice is thin, sweet, almost gentle. It says, in a perfectly human tongue, "Hello, Warden."

Tian Mo's mouth is dry.

"The door is open," says the rider. "The door is open. Come down and see."

"No," says Tian Mo.

"Then we shall come up."

The beast lunges.

* * *

He has fought a hundred crawlers in a night. He has fought Gnashers and Hunters and a thing with seven legs and a voice like a flute. He has never fought anything that fought back like this.

The Rider is fast. It is faster than anything of its size has any right to be. It comes up the stair like a wave, and the staff catches it across the shoulder, and it does not slow. A limb slams into his chest. He feels a rib crack. He is thrown against the wall, and the staff goes spinning, and the creature is on him, with its enormous blunt head lowered and its mouth wide.

He rolls. The jaws crash into the stone where his head had been. Chips fly. He gets a knee under him and drives a fist, bare, into the soft flesh behind the beast's jaw, and it screams.

It is the first time he has heard a sound like that. It is not an animal's scream. It is a person's.

The rider on its back is laughing.

He seizes the staff. He comes up under the Rider's chin with a short brutal swing, and the head snaps back, and the beast staggers. He drives forward. He does not think. He is Kuang, he is Hu, he is every man who ever stood on this step and refused to move, and he strikes with the whole weight of twenty-three years.

The Rider falls.

It goes down on its side, thrashing, and the rider is thrown clear, and the great limbs claw at the stone. The beast is not dead. It is huge, and furious, and half pinned, one limb snared in the crack where the stair meets the wall. It heaves. The wall groans.

The stone creature goes in first. It moves with a terrible, patient slowness, and it takes a limb of the Rider's beast in both hands and simply leans, as a man leans on a door. Bone cracks. The beast shrieks and tears free, leaving a gray hand still clamped around its joint, and the creature looks down at the stump of its own wrist with mild surprise, and then seizes the beast again with the other.

"Good," Tian Mo grunts. "Hold it."

He staggers up, one hand pressed to his ribs. Blood is running into his eye. Below him the pale rider has struggled to its feet and is crawling back toward the beast's flank, clawing for the harness, and he sees that if it reaches the sinew straps, the whole creature will rise. He cannot let that happen. Not here. Not with seven hundred children asleep behind him in the dark.

He sets his jaw and runs the three steps to the wall.

Tian Mo steps forward, to finish it.

He sees too late that the crack is not a crack. It is a mouth. It is the open jaw of a second beast, buried in the wall, a Gnasher that has been waiting in the stone since the first hour for a man to come close enough to bite.

The jaws close on his left arm.

He does not scream. He has no breath. He looks down, with a strange cold detachment, at the dark thing that has his arm from the elbow to the wrist, and feels the bone give, slowly, like the wood of a green branch. The pain does not come. Not yet. There is only an enormous pressure, and a sound in his ears, a long clear ringing note.

On the step above, the rider is rising. Its needle mouth is smiling.

"Hold," says the Gate wall, from the bottom of the world, very softly. "Hold. He is almost here."

Tian Mo tries to pull free.

He cannot move.
